analysis.body:
The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey recorded 36.8 percent of finance and insurance firms using AI in the most recent period, up from 35.5 percent in the prior period, making it one of the higher-adoption sectors in the broader economy. That figure covers the full finance and insurance grouping under NAICS 52, so the share specific to banking alone is not separately broken out in this data.

Banking is notable among industries because AI governance predates the current generative AI moment by more than a decade. Credit scoring and anti-money-laundering models have long operated under the Federal Reserve's SR 11-7 model risk management guidance, issued in 2011 and listed in the Fed's supervisory letters index. That framework requires banks to validate, document, and oversee quantitative models, which means the compliance infrastructure for governing AI already exists in most institutions, even if the tools themselves are changing rapidly.

The sector's current frontier is generative AI applied to customer service and compliance workflows, layered on top of the fraud-detection and credit models that have been running for decades. The Financial Models section on this site tracks the fifty most-downloaded open models tuned for financial text on the Hugging Face Hub, refreshed daily, which gives a view of where open-source development is concentrating in this domain.

A separate benchmark worth knowing is the Evident AI Banking Index, which scores major global banks across quantitative maturity metrics spanning talent, innovation, leadership, and transparency. It is described as the closest thing banking has to a public AI scoreboard, though the underlying scores are not reproduced in the data available here.

On the risk side, Treasury has framed the supervisory conversation through its report on AI in financial services, covering uses, opportunities, and risks for the sector. The page that was expected to carry that analysis instead returned content about OFAC sanctions related to gold smuggling and money laundering, so the specific findings from Treasury's AI report are not available to summarize from the harvested text.

For a reader weighing deployment, banking offers an unusual combination of mature regulatory scaffolding and relatively high measured adoption. The SR 11-7 framework means regulators already expect model inventories, validation processes, and clear ownership, so any new AI system, including generative tools, will likely need to fit inside that governance structure from day one rather than being retrofitted later.
